claims.text: Surface segregation of Cu initiates the phase-transition onset in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated Cu governs the progression of the phase transition.
Local Cu enrichment lowers the melting threshold at nanoparticle surfaces.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous.
Heating causes Cu to segregate to the nanoparticle surface because Cu has a lower melting point.
Cu-rich surface regions melt at lower temperatures than the bulk of the FeNiCrCoCu alloy.
Local melting nucleates a liquid-like phase at the nanoparticle surface.
The liquid-like phase progressively spreads from the surface into the nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles with Cu-rich surfaces will begin localized surface melting earlier than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with Cu-rich surfaces will have a lower overall melting point than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
An inert atmosphere or high vacuum minimizes oxidation during heating.
The proposed mechanism applies near and above the premelting regime when oxidation is minimal.
The mechanism may cease to apply below particle-size limits where diffusion kinetics are drastically altered.
Similar multicomponent nanoparticle studies show trends consistent with surface segregation and melting-point depression.
Nanoparticle size, strain, and local ordering may affect the magnitude of Cu enrichment and melting-temperature change.
